name: David Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying economics, and I take the early train in from my hometown, which is an hour each way. Most days it's lectures, then home, because I try not to spend money in the city. On Saturdays I work at my uncle's building supply yard, loading timber and bagging cement, and on Sunday morning I go to church with my family.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your hometown like for work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's small. A few shops, the yard, a factory that makes pallets and a care home. The older men say there used to be three factories. Most young people leave, and I'd like to stay near my parents, but I also want a proper career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one is called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted the hype. Computers are tools and tools don't replace good people. I'd say work hard, keep your head down, and things work out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd still be worried about money. My loan is large, the yard only gives me Saturdays, and there's nothing else nearby. Economics is a good degree, but my results are average and banks take the top ones. I'd be cautious and not count on luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am: study, the yard on Saturdays, and church. I'd try to get a few extra weekday hours from my uncle in the holidays. I'd apply for a job at the local bank branch or the council for a placement. I wouldn't touch AI at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, but with some pressure underneath. I like routine and I like knowing what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you still be cautious about money in a quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen what happens to families when one pay packet stops. My uncle had to lay off two men when the housing market dipped. I'd rather have a small amount saved than a big plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why don't you want to use AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like things I don't understand. If I can't explain how it got the answer, how can I put my name on it? My dad says a man's work should be his own, and I agree.

say: I'd say I never **trusted the hype** and that tools don't replace good people.
I'd say work hard and **keep your head down**.
think: I'm worried about **money**: a large loan and only Saturday work nearby.
My results are **average**, and banks take the top ones.
do: Keep studying, the **yard on Saturdays** and church.
Ask my uncle for **holiday hours** and apply to the bank or council.
feel: **Settled** on the surface, with pressure underneath.
S0.quote: I've seen what happens to families when one pay packet stops. My uncle had to lay off two men when the housing market dipped.
fieldNote: David's caution comes from **seeing his uncle** lay men off.
Refuses AI on principle and ties it to his father's view of honest work.
Wants to stay near his parents but knows jobs are scarce.

steps.text: Keep Saturdays at my uncle's building supply yard
Put a little into savings each week
Skip eating out in the city and bring lunch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one is called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be careful and not rush after every new thing. If jobs change, people should keep working and learning a trade. I'd say a stable job in a real business beats a risky idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think the office jobs I'm heading for might shrink. Banks and councils do a lot of checking and booking, which the card says AI takes first. But the yard, the care home and the factory still need people with hands, so some work stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree because I've started, and ask my uncle if there's more work for me over summer. I'd look at an apprenticeship in finance, because that way I learn on the job. I'd talk to my pastor and my dad about it. I'd stay away from AI as long as I can, but if an employer insisted, I'd learn it from someone I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncertain, a bit anxious. I don't like not knowing where I'll fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really avoid AI if a bank required it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd learn it, I'm not stupid. But I'd want to see my manager use it for a few weeks first. I'm slow at this stuff, but when I do learn something I keep it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if office jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that cut people to save money, and the government that lets them do it without making them train people. But I'd also blame young people who don't want to work with their hands, because that's where jobs survive.

say: I'd say we should be **careful** and not rush after every new thing.
I'd say a **stable job** beats a risky idea.
think: Office jobs in banks and councils might **shrink**.
The yard, the factory and the care home **still need hands**, so some work stays here at home.
do: Finish the degree and ask my uncle for **summer work**.
Look at a **finance apprenticeship** and talk to my pastor and dad.
feel: **Anxious**, because I don't like not knowing where I'll fit.
S1.quote: I'm slow at this stuff, but when I do learn something I keep it.
fieldNote: David's **resistance** is about trust and pace, not refusal.
Blames both companies and young people who avoid hands-on work.
Turns to his dad and pastor for decisions.

steps.text: Ask about finance apprenticeships at the local bank
Ask my uncle for more yard hours in summer
Talk the options through with my dad and pastor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one is called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong that it's allowed to happen this quickly. Companies and governments should have a duty to protect workers first. I'd say it at church and to my uncle's customers who come into the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think my degree would be worthless, and I'd be frightened. If AI does almost all thinking work by 2028, then banks, councils and offices don't need me. Hands-on work lasts until 2031, but robots follow. I wouldn't know where to put my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my uncle about full-time work at the yard, and to my dad about whether I should leave university. I'd keep my head down, save every pound, and ask the church whether there's any support. I'd look for a trade, like electrics, because a house still needs fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and angry. Like someone moved the goalposts when I was almost at the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what's the hardest decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether to carry on with my degree. I'd have a big loan for a thing that might not exist. But leaving also feels like a failure. I'd go and ask my pastor, because I need someone to say it's allowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I'm sorry, I thought the degree was the safe path and it isn't. My mum would cry, my dad would tell me to work with my hands. They'd both want me to stay close.

say: I'd say it's **wrong** to let this happen so quickly.
I'd say employers and government have a **duty to protect workers**.
think: My degree could be **worthless**, and I'd be frightened.
Hands-on work lasts until **2031**, but robots follow, and then I wouldn't know where to put my life.
do: Ask my uncle for **full-time yard work** and consider leaving university.
Train in a **trade like electrics** and ask the church for support.
feel: **Scared and angry**, as if someone moved the goalposts.
S2.quote: I'd go and ask my pastor, because I need someone to say it's allowed.
fieldNote: David's fear shows as **guilt** about leaving his degree.
Turns first to church and family rather than institutions.
Sees a trade as the only safe path.

steps.text: Ask my uncle for full-time work at the yard
Enrol on an electrics course at the local college
Ask the church about support for families
Sit down with my parents to decide about university

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one is called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and people should use it. I'd say go learn a trade or save some money. The stubborn ones will regret it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I could finish my degree, but the clock would be running. I'd graduate in 2029 and the thinking jobs would be gone by 2031. That leaves me two years to build something, and I'd rather not rely on a bank job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, but start working towards something solid alongside it: an evening course in bookkeeping or construction management, so I could run a yard like my uncle's. I'd save most of what I earn on Saturdays. I'd also keep going to church and talk with the older men, because they know how to get through bad times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd cope. A plan helps me sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would running a yard involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering, accounts, dealing with builders. A lot of it is the thinking work on the card, so the ordering and accounts would change by 2031. But the lifting and delivering would take longer, until about 2034, so there'd still be a place for someone who knows the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two is a hurry and I don't do well in a hurry. Five means I can do the course, test the idea, and have a back-up. I'm the sort who needs to slowly check every part of the plan.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning** and people should use it.
I'd say learn a **trade** or save money.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with only **two years** before thinking jobs go.
I'd rather not rely on a **bank job**.
do: Finish the degree and take an evening **bookkeeping or construction** course.
Save most of my **Saturday** earnings and learn from the older men.
feel: **Anxious**, but a plan helps me sleep.
S3.quote: Two is a hurry and I don't do well in a hurry.
fieldNote: David's **resistance** turns into slow, careful planning.
Sees the family yard as a place where local knowledge still matters.
Needs time to check each step before moving.

steps.text: Take an evening bookkeeping course in second year
Save most of my Saturday wages
Learn ordering and customer accounts at the yard
Ask my uncle about a share of the yard someday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one is called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and the best answer is to keep building something real. I'd tell people not to panic and not to ignore it. A family and a community are the things that stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I'd be fine if I work steadily. By 2036 I'd be twenty-eight, married perhaps, with a steady job. I'd still be afraid that I won't change fast enough, because I'm slow and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, get a job at the bank or the council, and save for a house near my parents. I'd learn what I have to, at the pace I can, when the time comes. I'd stay close to church and my uncle's yard so I always have a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Ten years gives me room, though I know I'd waste some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by wasting some of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put things off. I'd think, there's time, and then suddenly it's year eight. I need someone, like my pastor or my uncle, to ask me how I'm getting on, or I'd drift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we've got ten years, so let's pay off what you owe and keep working. I'd promise to stay nearby and help with the house. That matters more to them than my career.

say: I'd say ten years is long and the answer is to **build something real**.
I'd say family and **community** are what stay.
think: I'd be fine if I work **steadily**, but I'm slow and I know it.
I'm afraid I won't **change fast enough**.
do: Finish the degree, take a **bank or council job** and save for a house nearby.
Learn what I must at my pace and keep my **uncle's yard** as a fallback.
feel: **Calm** mostly, though I'd waste some of the time.
S4.quote: I'd put things off. I'd think, there's time, and then suddenly it's year eight.
fieldNote: David's concern is his own **slowness**, not the technology.
Wants his pastor or uncle to hold him accountable.
Stays tied to family and community as the centre of his plans.

steps.text: Finish the degree and apply to the local bank
Save for a house near my parents
Ask my pastor to check how I'm doing each year
Learn new tools only when work requires them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It leaves no time to find my feet, and I'd feel I'd wasted my parents' sacrifice. What would help is a steady job route like apprenticeships, family support, and a government that stops firms from dropping people with no notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that small towns are forgotten in this. We don't have big employers or lots of choices. A lot of us want to stay near our families and work, and we just need a real chance.

headlineQuote: We don't have big employers or lots of choices.
portrait: David, 18, studies **economics**, commutes an hour from his small hometown and works Saturdays at his uncle's building yard.
He never uses AI, distrusts what he can't explain, and trusts church, family and work with **hands**.
He's a traditional free-market conservative who blames firms and young people avoiding trades.
Thin money and few local jobs keep him wary, and the two-year warning leaves him alarmed.
With more time he slows down and plans carefully, but fears he'd put things off.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because he'd have no time and would feel he'd wasted his parents' sacrifice.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships**, family support and rules that stop firms dropping people with no notice.
